arXiv:2609.14621v1 [quant-ph] 13 Sep 2026
A pretty-tight converse on the classical capacity
of generalized amplitude-damping channels
Kun Fang
Affiliation: School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen,
Guangdong, 518172, China
September 13, 2026
Abstract
The classical capacity of a quantum channel is the highest rate at which classical information can be transmitted with vanishing error. Although the capacities of many fundamental quantum channels have been established, the capacity of the generalized amplitude-damping channel remains an open problem in quantum Shannon theory. In this work, we revisit a converse bound introduced by Brandão et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 106, 230502 (2011)], which upper-bounds the classical capacity in terms of a correlation measure. For the generalized amplitude-damping channel, we derive a relaxation of this measure that makes the converse bound efficiently computable. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that our bound is pretty tight in general and nearly coincides with the Holevo information at nonzero temperatures, significantly improving upon existing bounds across the entire parameter range.
Contents
1 Introduction
2 Generalized amplitude-damping channels
3 A converse bound for the classical capacity
4 Numerical comparison
References
A Optimality of the correlation penalties
1 Introduction
The classical capacity  $C({\cal N})$  of a quantum channel is the highest rate at
which classical information can be transmitted with vanishing error.
The Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland theorem gives
$\displaystyle C({\cal N})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\chi({\cal N}^{\otimes n}),$
(1)
where  $\chi$  denotes the Holevo information
[Hol73, Hol98, SW97]. Evaluating this
regularized expression generally requires an optimization over
arbitrarily many channel uses [Has09]. Even for qubit channels,
exact, computable expressions for communication capacities are known
only in special cases. In particular, determining the classical
capacity of the amplitude-damping channel over its entire parameter
range remains a major open problem in quantum Shannon theory.
The generalized amplitude-damping channel (GADC) extends amplitude
damping to a two-level system coupled to a thermal bath at nonzero
temperature [KSW20]. It is characterized by a
damping probability  $\gamma$  and an equilibrium occupation probability
$N$ . The channel describes the spin-relaxation ( $T_{1}$ ) process arising
from energy exchange with a thermal environment. Such relaxation is
also a source of noise in superconducting-circuit-based quantum
computing [CB08]. It can also be used to characterize losses in linear optical systems in the presence of low-temperature background noise [ZLW+17]. When the thermal bath
is at zero temperature, the GADC reduces to the
amplitude-damping channel.
Despite its simple structure, the classical capacity of the GADC remains
unknown in general. Earlier approaches include the entanglement-assisted
bound, evaluated for the GADC by Hou and Fang [HF07a], and
Filippov’s upper bound for nonunital qubit channels [Fil18].
Wang, Xie, and Duan introduced semidefinite-programming (SDP) bounds for general
quantum channels [WXD18].
Leditzky, Kaur, Datta, and Wilde developed bounds based on approximate
covariance and proximity to entanglement-breaking
channels [LKDW18].
Khatri, Sharma, and Wilde subsequently evaluated and compared these bounds
for the GADC, deriving an analytic expression for the SDP
bounds [KSW20].
Fang and Fawzi obtained further improvements using the geometric
Rényi divergence [FF21]. Fawzi, Shayeghi, and Ta subsequently developed a symmetry-reduced hierarchy
of multi-copy SDP bounds, obtaining small improvements for amplitude
damping [FST22].
A significant gap nevertheless remains between the resulting upper bounds
and the achievable one-copy Holevo information.
In this work, we revisit a converse bound by Brandão, Eisert,
Horodecki, and Yang [BEHY11]. It upper-bounds classical
capacity by output entropy minus an output–environment correlation measure.
For the GADC, we derive a computable relaxation of this measure that retains
its dependence on the input occupation probability.
We obtain complementary correlation penalties from measurements on the
environment and the output. Koashi–Winter duality [KW04]
and two-qubit concurrence formulas [KdMT+08, Woo98]
reduce the environment-measurement estimate to scalar minimization and
convexification. A fixed output measurement gives the second penalty,
which is already convex. At each input occupation, we subtract the larger
penalty from the output entropy before maximizing over that variable. The resulting bound improves the known bounds across the entire parameter range. Notably, the new bound is pretty tight
at positive temperature, where it nearly matches the
achievable Holevo information.
2 Generalized amplitude-damping channels
For  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$ , the GADC acts as
$\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}:\quad\rho(q,z)$
$\displaystyle:=\begin{pmatrix}1-q&z\\[5.69046pt]
z^{*}&q\end{pmatrix}\quad\longmapsto\quad\begin{pmatrix}1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,z\\[5.69046pt]
\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,z^{*}&t_{\gamma,N}(q)\end{pmatrix},$
(2)
where  $q\in[0,1]$ ,  $|z|^{2}\leqslant q(1-q)$ , and
$t_{\gamma,N}(q):=\gamma N+(1-\gamma)q$ .
The quantities  $q$  and  $t_{\gamma,N}(q)$  are the occupation probabilities of  $|1\rangle$
at the input and output, respectively.
Let  $V_{\gamma,N}:A\to BE$  be a Stinespring isometry, with output system
$B$  and environment system  $E$ . The channel and its complement satisfy
$\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}[V_{\gamma,N}\rho V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}],\qquad{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[V_{\gamma,N}\rho V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}].$
(3)
We write  $S$  for the von Neumann entropy in bits
and  $h_{2}(x)=-x\log_{2}x-(1-x)\log_{2}(1-x)$  for the binary entropy.
A qubit state  $\rho$  has eigenvalues  $(1\pm\sqrt{1-4\det\rho})/2$ ,
so  $S(\rho)=f(\det\rho)$ , where
$\displaystyle f(d)$
$\displaystyle=h_{2}\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4d}}{2}\right),\qquad 0\leqslant d\leqslant\frac{1}{4}.$
(4)
For a pure input,  $|z|^{2}=q(1-q)$ , so the determinant of the output state
in (2) is
$\displaystyle D_{\gamma,N}(q)$
$\displaystyle=\gamma\big[(1-\gamma)(q-N)^{2}+N(1-N)\big].$
(5)
The one-copy Holevo information provides the achievable benchmark
$\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})\leqslant C({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})$  and is given by
[HF07b, KSW20]
$\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})=\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-f(D_{\gamma,N}(q))\right].$
(6)
By Wootters’ formula [Woo98], the concurrence of the
normalized Choi state of  ${\cal A}_{\gamma,N}$  is
$\displaystyle c_{\gamma,N}$
$\displaystyle=\left[\sqrt{1-\gamma}-\gamma\sqrt{N(1-N)}\right]_{+},$
(7)
where  $[x]_{+}=\max\{x,0\}$ .
3 A converse bound for the classical capacity
We start from a converse bound by Brandão, Eisert,
Horodecki, and Yang [BEHY11]. It upper-bounds classical
capacity by output entropy minus an output–environment correlation measure.
They applied this framework to amplitude damping by fixing a particular choice of measurements
on the environment and numerically optimizing the resulting bound over
mixed-state input ensembles [BEHY11, Fig. 2].
This yielded nontrivial upper bounds below the maximal output entropy
for  $0<\gamma\leqslant 1/2$ .
Here, we exploit the structure of the GADC to reduce the computation to a scalar optimization and convexification problem, yielding a much more precise estimate.
In particular, we obtain two complementary penalties by measuring the environment or
the output, denoted by  $g_{\gamma,N}^{E}$  and  $g_{\gamma,N}^{B}$ , respectively.
Their superscripts identify which subsystem is measured. Using the
quantities from Section 2, define
$\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q)$
$\displaystyle:=\operatorname{co}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q),\quad\ell_{\gamma,N}(q):=\min_{0\leqslant\delta\leqslant q(1-q)}\left[f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)+(1-\gamma)\delta)-f(c_{\gamma,N}^{2}\delta)\right],$
(8)
$\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)$
$\displaystyle:=h_{2}\!\left(p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q)\right)+h_{2}\!\left(p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q)\right)-f(\gamma q(1-q)),$
(9)
where
$\displaystyle p_{\gamma,N}^{\pm}(q)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1\pm\gamma(q-N)-\sqrt{[1-\gamma(q+N)]^{2}+4\gamma(1-\gamma)qN}}{2}\in[0,1].$
(10)
Here  $\delta$  ranges over the possible input determinants at fixed  $q$ ,
and  $\operatorname{co}$  denotes the lower convex envelope on  $[0,1]$ .
Taking the larger penalty at each occupation gives the following bound.
Theorem 1.
For every  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$ , let
$\displaystyle U_{G}(\gamma,N)$
$\displaystyle:=\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)\}\right].$
(11)
Then for every positive integer  $n$ ,
$\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n})$
$\displaystyle\leqslant nU_{G}(\gamma,N),\qquad C({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})\leqslant U_{G}(\gamma,N).$
(12)
To bound the Holevo information for arbitrarily many channel uses, we
separate an output-entropy term from a penalty for output–environment
correlations. Step 1 lower-bounds this penalty by a sum of single-copy
$G$  measures, without assuming product inputs.
For the GADC, Step 2 upper-bounds the entropy term using the input
occupation probabilities. Steps 3 and 4 then lower-bound  $G^{E}$  and
$G^{B}$  by  $g_{\gamma,N}^{E}$  and  $g_{\gamma,N}^{B}$ , using two-qubit
entanglement formulas and a fixed output measurement, respectively.
Finally, concavity of the entropy bound and convexity of the penalties
reduce both estimates to the mean input occupation. Choosing the larger
penalty and optimizing over this single variable gives  $U_{G}(\gamma,N)$ .
Step 1: Bounding the Holevo information.
For a bipartite state  $\omega_{BE}$ , a classical correlation measure obtained
by measuring the system  $E$  is [HV01]
$\displaystyle C^{E}(\omega)$
$\displaystyle=S(\omega_{B})-\inf_{\{M_{x}\}}\sum_{x}p_{x}S(\omega_{B}^{x}),$
$\displaystyle p_{x}\omega_{B}^{x}$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}[(I_{B}\otimes M_{x})\omega],$
(13)
where the infimum is over POVMs on  $E$ .
Throughout, superscripts on  $C$ ,  $G$ , and  $g$  identify the measured subsystem.
The convex-roof extension of  $C^{E}$  is defined by [BEHY11]
$\displaystyle G^{E}(\omega)=\inf_{\omega=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\omega_{j}}\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}C^{E}(\omega_{j}).$
(14)
Exchanging  $B$  and  $E$  defines  $C^{B}$  and  $G^{B}$ , which instead
use measurements on the output system  $B$ .
Let  $V:A\to BE$  be a Stinespring isometry for an arbitrary channel
${\cal N}$ , and set  $\Omega=V^{\otimes n}\rho_{A^{n}}(V^{\dagger})^{\otimes n}$ .
It is known that
$\displaystyle\chi({\cal N}^{\otimes n})$
$\displaystyle=\max_{\rho_{A^{n}}}\left[S(B^{n})_{\Omega}-E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n}:E^{n})_{\Omega}\right]$
(15)
$\displaystyle\leqslant\max_{\rho_{A^{n}}}\left[S(B^{n})_{\Omega}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max\!\left\{G^{E_{i}}(\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}}),G^{B_{i}}(\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}})\right\}\right],$
(16)
where  $E_{F}$  is the entanglement of formation.
The equality is the Matsumoto–Shimono–Winter representation
[MSW04]. The inequality follows from
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n}:E^{n})_{\Omega}$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max\!\left\{G^{E_{i}}(\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}}),G^{B_{i}}(\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}})\right\}.$
(17)
To obtain this form, apply the chain rule
[BEHY11, Eq. (13)]
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n}:E^{n})_{\Omega}$
$\displaystyle\geqslant E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n-1}:E^{n-1})_{\Omega}+G^{E_{n}}(\Omega_{B_{n}E_{n}}).$
(18)
Exchanging the two global parties gives the same residual term with
$G^{B_{n}}$  in place of  $G^{E_{n}}$ .
We may therefore choose the larger term at each step and iterate.
Step 2: Estimating the output entropy.
We now take  ${\cal N}={\cal A}_{\gamma,N}$  and  $V=V_{\gamma,N}$ .
For an arbitrary input  $\rho_{A^{n}}$ , write the occupation of each marginal state as
$q_{i}=\langle 1|\rho_{A_{i}}|1\rangle$  and  $\bar{q}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}q_{i}$ .
The entropy term in (16)
satisfies
$\displaystyle S(B^{n})_{\Omega}$
$\displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{i}S(B_{i})_{\Omega}\leqslant\sum_{i}h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q_{i}))\leqslant nh_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(\bar{q})).$
(19)
The first inequality is entropy subadditivity. The second follows by
dephasing each output qubit in the energy basis, whose occupation
probability is  $t_{\gamma,N}(q_{i})$ . The last inequality uses the concavity
of binary entropy and the affine dependence of
$t_{\gamma,N}(q)$  on  $q$ .
Step 3: Penalty by measuring the environment system.
For any input state  $\rho(q,z)$ , let
$\omega(q,z)=V_{\gamma,N}\rho(q,z)V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}$  be the output on system  $BE$ . We will show that
$\displaystyle G^{E}(\omega(q,z))\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q).$
(20)
Let  $|\psi\rangle_{AR}$  purify  $\rho(q,z)$ , with  $R$  a qubit reference.
The state  $|\Psi\rangle_{BER}=(V_{\gamma,N}\otimes I_{R})|\psi\rangle_{AR}$  is pure
and has  $BE$  marginal  $\omega(q,z)$ . Writing  $\delta=\det\rho(q,z)$ ,
we obtain
$\displaystyle C^{E}(\omega(q,z))$
$\displaystyle=S(B)_{\omega}-E_{\mathrm{F}}(B:R)$
$\displaystyle=f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)+(1-\gamma)\delta)-f\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{C}(B:R)^{2}}{4}\right)$
$\displaystyle=f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)+(1-\gamma)\delta)-f(c_{\gamma,N}^{2}\delta)$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\ell_{\gamma,N}(q).$
(21)
Here  $\mathcal{C}$  denotes two-qubit concurrence, and the quantities on
$B:R$  are evaluated on the corresponding marginal of  $|\Psi\rangle$ .
The first equality is Koashi–Winter duality
[KW04, Corollary 2].
For the second equality, the output matrix in (2)
gives
$\displaystyle\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho(q,z))$
$\displaystyle=t_{\gamma,N}(q)[1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)]-(1-\gamma)|z|^{2}$
$\displaystyle=t_{\gamma,N}(q)[1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)]-(1-\gamma)q(1-q)+(1-\gamma)\delta$
$\displaystyle=D_{\gamma,N}(q)+(1-\gamma)\delta,$
(22)
where  $\delta=\det\rho(q,z)=q(1-q)-|z|^{2}$ .
The last line follows by substituting  $t_{\gamma,N}(q)$  and
(5), and the output entropy follows from
(4).
For the two-qubit marginal on  $BR$ , Wootters’ formula gives [Woo98]
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{F}}(B:R)$
$\displaystyle=h_{2}\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-\mathcal{C}(B:R)^{2}}}{2}\right)=f\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{C}(B:R)^{2}}{4}\right).$
(23)
For the last equality in (21), consider the normalized
Choi state
$J_{\gamma,N}=(\operatorname{id}_{R}\otimes{\cal A}_{\gamma,N})(|\Phi^{+}\rangle\!\langle\Phi^{+}|_{RA})$ ,
where  $|\Phi^{+}\rangle_{RA}=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ .
We have [Woo98]
$\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(J_{\gamma,N})$
$\displaystyle=\left[\sqrt{1-\gamma}-\gamma\sqrt{N(1-N)}\right]_{+}=c_{\gamma,N}.$
(24)
Consequently,
$\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(B:R)$
$\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}(J_{\gamma,N})\,\mathcal{C}(|\psi\rangle_{AR})=2c_{\gamma,N}\sqrt{\det\rho(q,z)}=2c_{\gamma,N}\sqrt{\delta}.$
(25)
The first equality is the concurrence factorization law for a pure
two-qubit input under a channel acting on one qubit
[KdMT+08]. The second uses
$\mathcal{C}(|\psi\rangle_{AR})=2\sqrt{\det\rho(q,z)}$ , since  $\rho(q,z)$  is
the reduced state of the input purification. Substituting this
concurrence into (23) yields
$E_{\mathrm{F}}(B:R)=f(c_{\gamma,N}^{2}\delta)$ , establishing the last equality in
(21). The final inequality follows from the minimization in
(8), since  $0\leqslant\delta\leqslant q(1-q)$ .
To pass from  $C^{E}$  to its convex roof  $G^{E}$ , consider any decomposition
$\omega(q,z)=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\omega_{j}$  with  $\lambda_{j}>0$ .
For any vector  $|v\rangle$  orthogonal to the range of  $V_{\gamma,N}$ ,
$\displaystyle 0=\langle v|\omega(q,z)|v\rangle=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\langle v|\omega_{j}|v\rangle.$
(26)
Every summand is nonnegative, so  $\langle v|\omega_{j}|v\rangle=0$  for each  $j$ .
Positivity then implies  $\omega_{j}|v\rangle=0$ , showing that each
$\omega_{j}$  is supported on the range of  $V_{\gamma,N}$ .
Thus  $\rho_{j}:=V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}\omega_{j}V_{\gamma,N}$  is a
normalized qubit state and
$\displaystyle\omega_{j}$
$\displaystyle=V_{\gamma,N}\rho_{j}V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger},\qquad\rho(q,z)=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\rho_{j}.$
(27)
The first identity uses the support property; the second follows by
applying  $V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\cdot)V_{\gamma,N}$  to the decomposition of  $\omega(q,z)$ .
Writing  $\rho_{j}=\rho(q_{j},z_{j})$  gives  $\omega_{j}=\omega(q_{j},z_{j})$
and  $\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q$ . We therefore obtain
$\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}C^{E}(\omega(q_{j},z_{j}))$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q_{j})\geqslant\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q_{j})\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q).$
(28)
The first inequality follows from (21),
the second from  $g_{\gamma,N}^{E}\leqslant\ell_{\gamma,N}$ ,
and the third from convexity and  $\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q$ .
Taking the infimum proves the lower bound in (20) for
arbitrary coherence.
Step 4: Penalty by measuring the output system.
We now prove the bound by measuring the output system  $B$ . We aim to show that
$\displaystyle G^{B}(\omega(q,z))$
$\displaystyle\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q).$
(29)
We first lower-bound  $C^{B}$  using a fixed measurement on  $B$ .
Symmetry and convexity then show that the resulting correlation is
minimized, at fixed  $q$ , by the diagonal input  $\rho(q,0)$ .
Finally, convexity in  $q$  allows us to pass from  $C^{B}$  to its convex
roof  $G^{B}$ .
Write  $z=|z|e^{i\theta}$  and let
$U_{\theta}=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})$ , choosing  $\theta=0$  when
$z=0$ . Then  $U_{\theta}\rho(q,z)U_{\theta}^{\dagger}=\rho(q,|z|)$ .
The channel action in (2) gives
${\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(U_{\theta}\rho U_{\theta}^{\dagger})=U_{\theta}{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho)U_{\theta}^{\dagger}$  for every input  $\rho$ .
By unitary equivalence of Stinespring dilations, there is an
environment unitary  $W_{\theta}$  such that
$\displaystyle\omega(q,|z|)$
$\displaystyle=(U_{\theta}\otimes W_{\theta})\omega(q,z)(U_{\theta}\otimes W_{\theta})^{\dagger},$
$\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,|z|))$
$\displaystyle=C^{B}(\omega(q,z)).$
(30)
The second identity holds because local unitaries preserve all
entropies and map the set of output measurements onto itself.
Thus a lower bound depending only on  $q$  can be proved with  $z$  real.
We measure  $B$  in the Pauli- $Y$  basis, with outcomes  $x\in\{0,1\}$
and projectors  $\Pi_{x}=(I+(-1)^{x}Y)/2$ .
Let  $p_{x}$  be the probability of outcome  $x$  and  $\omega_{E}^{x}$  the
corresponding normalized environment state. The correlation obtained
from this measurement is
$\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z))\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)$
$\displaystyle:=S(\omega_{E})-\sum_{x=0}^{1}p_{x}S(\omega_{E}^{x})=S\!\left({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho(q,z))\right)-f(\gamma\delta),$
(31)
where  $\delta=\det\rho(q,z)$ .
For real  $z$ , the channel action gives the outcome probabilities and
adjoint effects
$\displaystyle p_{x}$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_{x}\omega_{B})=\frac{1}{2},\qquad{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})=\frac{I+(-1)^{x}\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,Y}{2},\qquad\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})=\frac{\gamma}{4}.$
(32)
Both conditional environment states therefore have entropy
$\displaystyle S(\omega_{E}^{x})$
$\displaystyle=f\!\left(\frac{\det\rho(q,z)\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})}{p_{x}^{2}}\right)=f(\gamma\delta).$
(33)
Indeed, since  $\Pi_{x}$  is rank one,  $\omega_{E}^{x}$  has the same nonzero
spectrum as the trace-one  $2\times 2$  matrix
$\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}\,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(\Pi_{x})\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}/p_{x}$ .
This is the standard equality of the nonzero spectra of  $AA^{\dagger}$
and  $A^{\dagger}A$ ; the entropy then follows from
(4). This proves
(31).
We next show why the diagonal input gives a lower bound at fixed  $q$ .
The measured correlation admits the relative-entropy representation
$\displaystyle C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x=0}^{1}D(\omega_{E}^{x}\|\omega_{E}),$
(34)
where  $D(\sigma\|\tau)=\operatorname{Tr}[\sigma(\log_{2}\sigma-\log_{2}\tau)]$ .
On the convex set of inputs with real coherence,  $p_{x}=1/2$  for both
outcomes. In particular,
$\displaystyle\omega_{E}^{x}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[(\Pi_{x}\otimes I_{E})\omega(q,z)]}{p_{x}}=2\operatorname{Tr}_{B}[(\Pi_{x}\otimes I_{E})\omega(q,z)].$
(35)
The unnormalized conditional state depends linearly on the input,
and division by the constant  $p_{x}=1/2$  preserves this dependence.
Thus both  $\omega_{E}$  and  $\omega_{E}^{x}$  depend affinely on  $\rho(q,z)$ .
Joint convexity of relative entropy therefore makes  $C_{Y}^{B}$  convex
in  $(q,z)$  on the real-coherence plane.
Moreover, conjugating the input by Pauli  $Z$  changes  $z$  to  $-z$ ,
interchanges outcomes  $0$  and  $1$ , and induces a unitary on  $E$ .
The measured correlation is therefore unchanged, and
$\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z))$
$\displaystyle\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)=\frac{C_{Y}^{B}(q,z)+C_{Y}^{B}(q,-z)}{2}\geqslant C_{Y}^{B}(q,0).$
(36)
The first inequality uses the fixed measurement, the equality uses
the symmetry, and the last inequality uses convexity together with
$\rho(q,0)=[\rho(q,z)+\rho(q,-z)]/2$ .
Equation (30) extends this lower bound
on  $C^{B}$  to every complex  $z$ , with the same occupation  $q$ .
The convexity argument concerns the full measured correlation, not its
two entropy terms separately.
For the diagonal input  $\rho(q,0)$ , choose a four-dimensional Kraus
realization, which does not change the complementary-output entropy.
With  $a=\gamma(1-N)q$  and  $b=\gamma N(1-q)$ , the environment state
takes the block form
$\displaystyle\omega_{E}$
$\displaystyle=a\oplus b\oplus\begin{pmatrix}(1-N)(1-\gamma q)&\sqrt{(1-\gamma)N(1-N)}\\
\sqrt{(1-\gamma)N(1-N)}&N(1-\gamma+\gamma q)\end{pmatrix}.$
(37)
The  $2\times 2$  block has trace  $1-a-b$  and determinant  $ab$ .
The full spectrum thus factors into binary distributions with
probabilities  $p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q)$  and  $p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q)$
from (10).
Using (33) with
$\delta=q(1-q)$  gives
$\displaystyle C_{Y}^{B}(q,0)$
$\displaystyle=h_{2}(p_{\gamma,N}^{+}(q))+h_{2}(p_{\gamma,N}^{-}(q))-f(\gamma q(1-q))=g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q).$
(38)
Finally,  $g_{\gamma,N}^{B}$  is convex in  $q$ , because it is the
restriction of the convex function  $C_{Y}^{B}$  to diagonal inputs.
By the decomposition argument in Step 3, every ensemble for
$\omega(q,z)$  has components  $\omega(q_{j},z_{j})$  with
$\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q$ . Hence
$\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}C^{B}(\omega(q_{j},z_{j}))$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q_{j})\geqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q).$
(39)
The first inequality uses the lower bound just established; the second uses convexity.
Taking the infimum over all decompositions proves
(29), without any further
convexification of  $g_{\gamma,N}^{B}$ .
Each marginal  $\Omega_{B_{i}E_{i}}$  has the form  $\omega(q_{i},z_{i})$ .
Combining the environment-measurement and output-measurement bounds with
(17) gives
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{F}}(B^{n}:E^{n})_{\Omega}$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\sum_{i}\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q_{i}),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q_{i})\}\geqslant n\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(\bar{q}),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(\bar{q})\}.$
(40)
The last inequality follows because the maximum of two convex
functions is convex. Both terms in the Holevo bound are now controlled
by the same mean occupation  $\bar{q}$ .
Substituting (19) and
(40) into (15) gives
$\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n})$
$\displaystyle\leqslant n\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-\max\{g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q),g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)\}\right]=nU_{G}(\gamma,N).$
(41)
Dividing by  $n$  and using (1) proves the capacity bound. This concludes the proof of Theorem 1.
Appendix A shows that both correlation
penalties are exact on diagonal inputs and hence are the largest
lower bounds on the respective  $G$  measures that depend only on  $q$ .
4 Numerical comparison
We compare  $U_{G}$  in (11) with the achievable Holevo rate
$\chi$  in (6) and two previous benchmarks.
These are the envelope of bounds collected and evaluated for the GADC by
Khatri, Sharma, and Wilde [KSW20], and the later
Fang–Fawzi bound [FF21]:
$\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{KSW}}(\gamma,N)$
$\displaystyle:=\min\{C_{\beta},C_{\mathrm{cov}},C_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}},C_{\mathrm{Fil}},C_{E}\},$
(42)
$\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{FF}}(\gamma,N)$
$\displaystyle:=\widehat{\Upsilon}_{1+2^{-10}}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}).$
(43)
The SDP bounds  $C_{\beta}$  were introduced by Wang, Xie,
and Duan [WXD18]; their equality and analytic evaluation
for the GADC were established in [KSW20].
The bounds  $C_{\mathrm{cov}}$  and  $C_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}}$  use
the approximate-covariance and approximate-entanglement-breaking methods
of Leditzky, Kaur, Datta, and Wilde [LKDW18].
The term  $C_{\mathrm{Fil}}$  is Filippov’s nonunital-qubit
bound [Fil18].
Finally,  $C_{E}$  is the entanglement-assisted classical
capacity [BSST02, Hol02], with the
GADC evaluation due to Hou and Fang [HF07a].
In our implementation,  $C_{\mathrm{EB}}^{\mathrm{TP}}$  uses a
trace-preserving entanglement-breaking comparison channel, and
$C_{\mathrm{Fil}}$  follows the population convention
in [Fil18].
The Fang–Fawzi bound  $U_{\mathrm{FF}}$  uses geometric Rényi
divergence at order  $1+2^{-10}$  [FF21].
Conjugating the input and output
by the Pauli operator  $X$  exchanges  $N$  and  $1-N$ , so the capacity is
symmetric under this exchange. We therefore restrict numerical
comparisons to  $N\leqslant 1/2$ .
Figure 1 presents six representative values of  $N$ ,
with  $U_{\mathrm{KSW}}$  and  $U_{\mathrm{FF}}$  shown separately. The improvement is clear and significant, providing almost tight estimation when  $N>0$ .
Figure 2 shows the heatmap for the residual gap  $U_{G}-\chi$ .
The capacity equals (6) at  $\gamma=0,1$ , on the unital
line  $N=1/2$ , and in the entanglement-breaking region
[KSW20]
$\displaystyle 1-\gamma\leqslant\gamma^{2}N(1-N).$
(44)
Our bound also recovers equality throughout this region. Indeed,
(44) gives  $c_{\gamma,N}=0$ , so
$\ell_{\gamma,N}(q)=f(D_{\gamma,N}(q))$ .
This function is convex in  $q$ , since  $2\sqrt{D_{\gamma,N}(q)}$  is convex
and  $x\mapsto f(x^{2}/4)$  is convex and increasing [Woo98].
Thus  $g_{\gamma,N}^{E}=\ell_{\gamma,N}$ , and
Theorem 1 yields
$U_{G}(\gamma,N)=\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})$ .
Figure 1: Classical-capacity bounds at
different values of  $N$ .
The upper bound  $U_{G}$  is compared with the Holevo rate  $\chi$ , the bound
$U_{\mathrm{KSW}}$  in [KSW20], and the
Fang–Fawzi bound  $U_{\mathrm{FF}}$  in [FF21].
Figure 2: Residual gap  $U_{G}-\chi$ , in bits per channel use. Numerical contours mark gaps of  $10^{-1}$ ,  $10^{-2}$ ,  $10^{-3}$ ,  $10^{-4}$ ,  $10^{-5}$ ,
and  $10^{-6}$  bits. The orange
curve marks the entanglement-breaking boundary in (44).

Appendix A Optimality of the correlation penalties
We show that the penalties in Theorem 1 are optimal
among lower bounds depending only on the input occupation.
Fix  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$  and write
$\omega(q,z)=V_{\gamma,N}\rho(q,z)V_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}$ .
Proposition 2 (Optimality at fixed input occupation).
For every  $q\in[0,1]$  and  $M\in\{E,B\}$ ,
$\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{M}(q)$
$\displaystyle=G^{M}(\omega(q,0))=\min_{|z|^{2}\leqslant q(1-q)}G^{M}(\omega(q,z)).$
(45)
The environment-measurement penalty is attained by pairing opposite
coherences and convexifying over the input occupation. For the
output-measurement penalty, equality follows from optimality of the
Pauli- $Y$  measurement, which we establish first.
Lemma 3 (Optimal output measurement).
For every input state  $\rho(q,z)$ ,
$\displaystyle C^{B}(\omega(q,z))$
$\displaystyle=S\!\left({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{c}(\rho(q,z))\right)-f\!\left(\gamma\det\rho(q,z)\right).$
(46)
If  $z$  is real, measuring  $B$  in the Pauli- $Y$  basis is optimal.
For a diagonal input, every equatorial projective measurement is optimal.
Proof.
Let  $\delta=\det\rho(q,z)$ . If  $\delta=0$ , any rank-one output measurement
leaves pure conditional environment states, and the claim follows from
$f(0)=0$ . We therefore assume  $\delta>0$ .
Refining a POVM cannot increase the average conditional entropy, so it
suffices to consider rank-one effects on  $B$ . Write these as
$M_{x}=w_{x}(I+\bm{n}_{x}\cdot\bm{\sigma})$ , where
$\bm{\sigma}=(X,Y,Z)$ ,  $w_{x}\geqslant 0$ ,  $|\bm{n}_{x}|=1$ ,
$\sum_{x}w_{x}=1$ , and  $\sum_{x}w_{x}\bm{n}_{x}=0$ .
With  $u_{x}=n_{x,z}$ , the channel action gives
$\displaystyle\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})$
$\displaystyle=\gamma w_{x}^{2}\left([1+(1-2N)u_{x}]^{2}+4(1-\gamma)N(1-N)u_{x}^{2}\right)$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\gamma w_{x}^{2}[1+(1-2N)u_{x}]^{2}.$
(47)
Consequently,
$\displaystyle\sum_{x}\sqrt{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})}$
$\displaystyle\geqslant\sqrt{\gamma}\sum_{x}w_{x}[1+(1-2N)u_{x}]=\sqrt{\gamma}.$
(48)
Here  $1+(1-2N)u_{x}\geqslant 0$ , and the equality uses POVM completeness.
Let  $p_{x}$  and  $\omega_{E}^{x}$  denote the outcome probabilities and
normalized conditional environment states.
The direct spectral argument in Step 4 applies to each rank-one
effect  $M_{x}$ : the nonzero spectrum of  $\omega_{E}^{x}$  equals that of
$\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}\,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})\sqrt{\rho(q,z)}/p_{x}$ .
This  $2\times 2$  matrix has trace one, so
$\displaystyle S(\omega_{E}^{x})$
$\displaystyle=f\!\left(\delta\,\frac{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})}{p_{x}^{2}}\right).$
(49)
Zero-probability outcomes have vanishing adjoint effects and are omitted
from conditional-state sums. It follows that
$\displaystyle\sum_{x}p_{x}S(\omega_{E}^{x})$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{x}p_{x}f\!\left(\delta\,\frac{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})}{p_{x}^{2}}\right)\geqslant f\!\left(\delta\left[\sum_{x}\sqrt{\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\dagger}(M_{x})}\right]^{2}\right)\geqslant f(\gamma\delta).$
(50)
The first inequality uses (49)
and convexity of  $s\mapsto f(s^{2})$  on  $[0,1/2]$  [Woo98].
The second uses monotonicity and (48).
For real  $z$ , the Pauli- $Y$  measurement attains equality by
(33); phase covariance
supplies the corresponding rotated measurement for complex  $z$ .
When  $z=0$ , every equatorial projective measurement has probabilities
$1/2$  and adjoint-effect determinants  $\gamma/4$ , so all are optimal.
∎
Proof of Proposition 2.
By (20) and (29), it suffices
to prove that both lower bounds are attained at  $z=0$ .
1. Environment-measurement penalty.
For any  $\varepsilon>0$ , the definition of the lower convex envelope
provides a finite ensemble  $\{\lambda_{j},q_{j}\}$  such that
$\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}$
$\displaystyle=1,\qquad\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}q_{j}=q,\qquad\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q_{j})\leqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q)+\varepsilon.$
(51)
Choose a minimizing determinant  $\delta_{j}$  in (8),
which exists by continuity on a compact interval, and set
$z_{j}=\sqrt{q_{j}(1-q_{j})-\delta_{j}}$ .
Then
$\displaystyle C^{E}(\omega(q_{j},z_{j}))$
$\displaystyle=C^{E}(\omega(q_{j},-z_{j}))=\ell_{\gamma,N}(q_{j}).$
(52)
$\displaystyle\omega(q,0)$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\frac{\lambda_{j}}{2}\left[\omega(q_{j},z_{j})+\omega(q_{j},-z_{j})\right].$
(53)
The correlation identity follows from (21), and the
decomposition follows by cancellation of opposite coherences.
Evaluating the convex roof on this decomposition gives
$\displaystyle G^{E}(\omega(q,0))$
$\displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\ell_{\gamma,N}(q_{j})\leqslant g_{\gamma,N}^{E}(q)+\varepsilon.$
(54)
Mixed components are allowed in (14).
Letting  $\varepsilon\to 0$  proves the claim for  $G^{E}$ .
2. Output-measurement penalty.
For a diagonal input,
$\displaystyle g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q)$
$\displaystyle\leqslant G^{B}(\omega(q,0))\leqslant C^{B}(\omega(q,0))=g_{\gamma,N}^{B}(q).$
(55)
The inequalities use (29) and the
single-component decomposition in the convex roof. The equality follows
from Lemma 3 and
(9).
